title: In utero reversal of placental insufficiency

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that reverses established placental insufficiency while pregnancy continues. The placenta would recover enough of its ability to support fetal growth and development that placental disease no longer requires early delivery. In pregnancies with preeclampsia, treatment would also need to resolve the associated maternal endothelial syndrome—the dysfunction of blood-vessel lining that contributes to maternal illness. These are connected but distinct targets: isolated placental fetal growth restriction need not include a maternal endothelial syndrome.

The intended scope is placental insufficiency underlying early preeclampsia or placental fetal growth restriction. It does not encompass every cause of fetal growth restriction, chronic hypertension, or every hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Its defining advance would be disease modification after placental disease has begun, beyond preventing some cases, controlling blood pressure or seizures, or changing a circulating biomarker. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate that this capability has been achieved.

significance.text: The 2023 reviews describe delivery as the only definitive cure for preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. When severe placental disease develops early, delivery can exchange the risks of continued pregnancy for the risks of serious prematurity. Safely reversing the disease in utero would introduce a fundamentally different option: treating the dysfunctional placenta in place while allowing pregnancy to continue. Avoiding otherwise indicated early delivery would follow directly from a successful demonstration of that capability.

Preeclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, and fetal growth restriction is associated with adverse outcomes before and after birth. A successful treatment could reduce maternal crises, improve fetal growth, and reduce harm associated with prematurity. Those benefits, and their magnitude, would need to be measured in clinical studies; extra time in pregnancy is valuable only if maternal and fetal health remain sufficiently protected.

The potential impact has important boundaries. Survivors of preeclampsia have increased later cardiovascular risk, but the supplied evidence does not establish preeclampsia as a leading cause of later cardiovascular disease or show that reversing the pregnancy syndrome would prevent that later disease. Similarly, delivery ends dependence on the dysfunctional placenta without necessarily immediately resolving maternal illness or reversing fetal injury already sustained. An in-utero treatment would need separate evidence for durable maternal and child benefits.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated recovery of placental support for the fetus and, where present, resolution of maternal disease after onset. Human preeclampsia has an incompletely defined aetiology. A dysfunctional placenta releases factors that contribute to maternal endothelial dysfunction, including the antiangiogenic factor soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, or sFlt-1. Identifying a contributor to maternal illness does not establish that removing it repairs the placental processes responsible for inadequate fetal support.

The 2026 selective sFlt-1 removal pilot illustrates this distinction. It reported changes in circulating sFlt-1 and maternal blood pressure, but the supplied abstract does not establish restored placental exchange, normalized fetal growth, resolution of the whole maternal syndrome, or safe continuation to term. Its findings cannot settle whether every possible strategy targeting an antiangiogenic signal would succeed or fail.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing therapy must connect a biological intervention to sustained organ function and clinical safety. Concrete barriers include determining which established placental injuries remain reversible, identifying pregnancies likely to respond, distinguishing improvement in maternal circulating signals from recovery of fetal support, and maintaining benefit without exposing the mother or fetus to unacceptable treatment risks. Different presentations may require different interventions; a treatment effective for one placental disease subgroup would not establish efficacy across all placental insufficiency.

current_state.text: Dimitriadis and colleagues’ review, published on 16 February 2023 in Nature Reviews Disease Primers, describes treatment directed at hypertension and seizures while identifying delivery of the placenta and baby as the only definitive cure for preeclampsia, often at a premature gestation. Giouleka and colleagues’ November 2023 review of major fetal-growth-restriction guidelines in Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey likewise describes delivery as the only definitive cure. These are dated descriptions of the therapeutic gap, rather than proof of treatment availability or absence at every subsequent date.

Prevention has demonstrated efficacy in a defined population. In Rolnik and colleagues’ 2017 randomized aspirin-versus-placebo trial in pregnancies screened as high risk, treatment began at 11–14 weeks and continued until 36 weeks. Preterm preeclampsia occurred in 13 participants receiving aspirin, or 1.6%, compared with 35 receiving placebo, or 4.3%; the reported odds ratio was 0.38. Disease still occurred, and the trial addressed prevention before onset rather than reversal of established placental disease.

Thadhani and colleagues’ 2026 Nature Medicine report describes an investigational, single-arm, open-label pilot of selective sFlt-1 removal by apheresis in very preterm preeclampsia, with safety and tolerability as its primary endpoints. In the nine-person multiple-dose phase B cohort, each apheresis reduced sFlt-1 by 16.7 ± 7.6% and mean arterial pressure by 4.1 ± 7.8 mmHg. Pregnancy continued from admission for a median of 10 days, with a range of 3–19 days. These quantitative findings apply to that phase B cohort and should not be generalized to all pilot participants.

The observed time from admission to delivery is not a demonstrated treatment-attributable extension of pregnancy: the uncontrolled design cannot establish how long those pregnancies would otherwise have continued. The pilot supports further investigation of selective sFlt-1 removal, and its authors call for controlled trials to assess additional safety and efficacy. It does not establish reversal that removes the need for disease-driven early delivery, normalized fetal growth, or safe continuation to term.

Evidence-access limitation: the supplied review assessed abstracts rather than the complete articles for all four sources. The aspirin URL requested full text but resolved to an abstract page. The retained pages were reported as untruncated and without extraction issues, but that does not make them complete article texts; detailed methods and outcomes beyond the reviewed abstracts cannot be assumed.

Evidence-coverage limitation: although the source index records retrieval on 1 November 2026, the supplied material contains no bounded freshness search establishing that these were the latest results or that no qualifying treatment was available through that date. The record therefore documents a therapeutic gap in the 2023 reviews and an investigational approach in 2026, while leaving the exhaustive present-day availability question unresolved. This limitation does not invalidate the reported dated findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: enroll pregnancies with clearly defined early-onset preeclampsia or severe early fetal growth restriction attributable to placental insufficiency, and compare a prespecified treatment with a concurrent control. The study should demonstrate sustained recovery of placental support and fetal growth, resolution of maternal disease when present, and continuation into a prespecified gestational range associated with substantially less serious prematurity. The goal is to remove the placental disease indication for early delivery within the demonstrated population; reaching term need not be the only meaningful endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained placental recovery removes disease indication for early delivery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and efficacy requirements: define numerical gestational targets, fetal-growth and maternal-disease endpoints, acceptable safety margins, rescue-delivery rules, follow-up periods, and adequate statistical power before testing. Benefit should not come with an unacceptable increase in stillbirth, maternal organ failure, or serious neonatal harm. A biomarker reduction, modest blood-pressure change, or a few observed additional days in a single-arm study would not by itself demonstrate disease reversal.
completion_criteria.label: Numerical efficacy targets and safety margins defined before testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: confirm benefit across independent studies or centers, characterize response by gestational age and placental disease presentation, and establish a treatment schedule that can be delivered safely during pregnancy. Follow-up should assess whether maternal recovery persists and whether children benefit beyond delayed delivery. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards. Finite trials would establish demonstrated efficacy and safety within their studied populations, rather than universal reversibility of placental insufficiency.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies confirm benefit and define safe treatment schedules

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock, overlaps in the aim of extending pregnancy. Its target is the timing of labor; OBG-04 targets placental dysfunction that can require delivery even when spontaneous labor has not begun. Suppressing labor would not itself establish restored placental support or resolution of maternal disease.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, addresses another route to premature birth. Repairing membranes or restoring the amniotic compartment would not itself repair placental exchange, while placental recovery would not demonstrate membrane repair. Both capabilities could matter in a pregnancy with more than one complication, but they require distinct demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, shares the goal of reducing harm when pregnancy cannot continue safely. OBG-03 concerns support outside the uterus; OBG-04 seeks to preserve a safe intrauterine pregnancy by reversing the placental disease that would otherwise prompt delivery. Success in either would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease, also proposes treatment before birth, but targets a molecular cause of fetal disease. OBG-04 targets the placenta and associated maternal illness. Improved fetal growth after placental treatment would not demonstrate correction of a fetal genetic disorder.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, overlaps in the broader challenge of sustaining gestation. Its defining capability is a manufactured uterine environment; OBG-04 concerns recovery of a dysfunctional placenta during an existing pregnancy. Neither capability implies the other.

Aspirin prevention is a relevant clinical comparator rather than an equivalent breakthrough. The supplied randomized trial demonstrates reduced preterm preeclampsia incidence in screened high-risk pregnancies when treatment begins before disease onset. OBG-04 requires treatment after placental disease has become established. Prevention remains clinically valuable, but it answers a different therapeutic question.

change_log.change: Preserved OBG-04 and its title while defining reversal as recovery of placental fetal support and resolution of maternal disease when present.
change_log.reason: This retains the innovation’s identity while distinguishing isolated placental fetal growth restriction from preeclampsia with a maternal endothelial syndrome.

change_log.change: Restricted fetal-growth-restriction scope to placental causes and distinguished chronic hypertension and other hypertensive disorders.
change_log.reason: Fetal growth restriction has heterogeneous causes, and the proposed placental intervention does not imply treatment of every growth or blood-pressure disorder.

change_log.change: Replaced an exhaustive claim about failed antiangiogenic blockade with the specific findings and limits of selective sFlt-1 removal.
change_log.reason: The pilot does not test all signal-blocking strategies or establish restored placental exchange or safe continuation to term.

change_log.change: Specified that the 2026 quantitative results concern the nine-person multiple-dose phase B cohort and added the reported blood-pressure change.
change_log.reason: The review supports cohort-specific reductions of 16.7 ± 7.6% in sFlt-1 and 4.1 ± 7.8 mmHg in mean arterial pressure.

change_log.change: Distinguished the median 10-day observed continuation from treatment-attributable pregnancy prolongation.
change_log.reason: A single-arm study lacks the concurrent comparison needed to establish causal extension.

change_log.change: Corrected the later cardiovascular claim to increased risk and separated possible long-term benefit from demonstrated outcomes.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not support a leading-cause ranking or establish that treating the pregnancy syndrome prevents later cardiovascular disease.

change_log.change: Clarified that delivery does not necessarily immediately resolve all maternal illness or reverse fetal consequences.
change_log.reason: Ending dependence on the dysfunctional placenta is distinct from complete recovery from its effects.

change_log.change: Preserved the aspirin trial’s event counts, rates, odds ratio, and treatment timing while distinguishing prevention from reversal.
change_log.reason: The randomized evidence concerns screened high-risk pregnancies treated before disease onset.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include reproducibility, prespecified outcomes, safety boundaries, rescue delivery, follow-up, and population limits.
change_log.reason: These details make a convincing demonstration assessable without presenting proposed criteria as established standards.

change_log.change: Retained abstract-access and freshness limitations and separated them from the validity of dated findings.
change_log.reason: Complete retained webpages are not complete articles, and retrieval dates do not establish an exhaustive search through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Integrated relevant roster distinctions and labeled unsourced engineering reasoning and proposed demonstrations explicitly.
change_log.reason: This preserves related concepts as separate entries and distinguishes source-backed findings from synthesis.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether a qualifying treatment remained unavailable through 1 November 2026; no bounded freshness search was supplied.

Full article methods and outcomes were not available in the reviewed evidence. The abstract-level record cannot resolve additional details of participant selection, safety, fetal outcomes, or follow-up.
It remains unresolved whether selective sFlt-1 removal produces sustained placental recovery or clinically meaningful benefits beyond the biochemical and blood-pressure changes reported in the pilot.
Which placental disease subtypes and stages remain reversible, and whether maternal and fetal responses can be restored together, remain open questions.

Numerical gestational targets, disease-resolution definitions, fetal-growth endpoints, safety margins, sample sizes, and follow-up durations remain to be specified for an actual demonstration protocol.
Any effect of successful in-utero reversal on later maternal cardiovascular disease or long-term child health would require separate evidence.

brief.title: Repairing the placenta during pregnancy
possible: A pregnancy threatened by a failing placenta—the organ that supports the growing baby—could continue safely after treatment restores its function. For early preeclampsia, a pregnancy illness involving high blood pressure and other complications, treatment would also resolve the mother's illness.
why: Families facing severe placental disease early in pregnancy could gain an option beyond early delivery. Restoring the placenta could improve the baby's growth, reduce maternal crises and avoid harm from being born too soon.

sources.showed: Their review described how a dysfunctional placenta causes maternal illness in preeclampsia. It identified delivery as the only cure, with available treatments targeting blood pressure and seizures.
sources.cited_for: The review explains why treating maternal symptoms alone does not reverse placental disease.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a treatment that restores placental function during pregnancy.

sources.showed: Their review compared guidelines for fetal growth restriction, when a baby grows too slowly before birth. It found agreement on some aspects of care but differences in definitions and monitoring.
sources.quote: Several discrepancies were identified regarding the definition of FGR and small-for-gestational-age fetuses, the diagnostic criteria, and the need of testing for congenital infections.
sources.cited_for: The review describes delivery as the only definitive cure for fetal growth restriction.
sources.not_established: The review does not show that treatment can restore growth by repairing the placenta.

sources.showed: A randomized trial found that low-dose aspirin reduced preeclampsia requiring early delivery in pregnancies screened as high risk.
sources.quote: Treatment with low-dose aspirin in women at high risk for preterm preeclampsia resulted in a lower incidence of this diagnosis than placebo.
sources.cited_for: The trial establishes that prevention can reduce disease in a defined high-risk population.
sources.not_established: Treatment began before disease developed, so the trial does not establish reversal after onset.

sources.showed: A small pilot used apheresis, a blood-filtering procedure, to remove sFlt-1, a placental protein contributing to maternal illness. Repeated treatment lowered this protein and blood pressure.
sources.quote: Compared to antenatal estimated birth weights, neonatal birth weights generally remained stable or increased among those with the longest extensions.
sources.cited_for: The pilot demonstrates targeted protein removal and accompanying blood-pressure changes.
sources.not_established: Without a comparison group, the pilot cannot establish that treatment delayed delivery or restored placental support.

shown: Thadhani and colleagues tested targeted blood filtering in very early preeclampsia. The repeated-treatment group included nine women. The pilot focused on safety and tolerability; it has not demonstrated recovery sufficient to remove the need for early delivery.
missing: Treatment must restore sustained placental support and fetal growth after disease begins, while resolving maternal illness where present.
Controlled trials must establish that continuing pregnancy reduces serious prematurity without unacceptable harm to mother or baby.

milestones.label: Placental recovery removes the need for early delivery
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show sustained placental and fetal growth recovery, maternal recovery where needed, and continuation to a less premature stage. This would establish reversal in the pregnancies studied.

milestones.label: Numerical success targets and safety limits are set beforehand
milestones.explanation: Trials would need numerical outcome targets, safety limits, emergency delivery rules, follow-up plans and enough participants set before testing. These would distinguish meaningful recovery from small changes in blood tests or pressure.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm benefit and safe treatment schedules
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm benefit, identify who responds and establish safe schedules, with follow-up of mothers and children. This would define where treatment works and whether benefits last.

uncertain: Which forms and stages of placental damage remain reversible, and can maternal recovery and fetal growth improve together?
The pregnancy-duration targets, definitions of recovery and acceptable safety margins still need to be specified.
Whether reversal would improve long-term child health or reduce mothers' later cardiovascular disease remains unknown.

page.title: Reversal of placental insufficiency in utero
page.definition: Treatment restores placental oxygen and nutrient supply after insufficiency develops, sustaining fetal growth without disease-driven preterm delivery. For early preeclampsia, a pregnancy disorder involving hypertension and organ or placental dysfunction, it also resolves the maternal syndrome while pregnancy continues.

goal.need: A 2019 estimate put severe early-onset fetal growth restriction at 11,000 babies a year in the EU. A fetus receiving too little oxygen risks brain injury or stillbirth. Delivering very early adds risks of brain haemorrhage and chronic lung disease. In pre-eclampsia, blood-pressure treatment and seizure prevention protect the mother while the placenta can continue to drive disease. Restoring placental support could give the baby time to grow and mature, provided both mother and fetus can safely continue the pregnancy.

statements.context: The consortium’s final report states this purpose for translating a maternal gene therapy into clinical use. FGR means fetal growth restriction.

delay or stop maternal disease progression

completion.title: Treatment reverses established placental disease and removes its indication for preterm delivery.
completion.criterion: In pregnancies with established placental insufficiency, a randomized controlled trial demonstrates recovery of placental support sufficient to sustain fetal growth and remove the disease indication for delivery before 37 weeks. Where pre-eclampsia is present, the hypertension, proteinuria and other organ dysfunction attributable to pre-eclampsia resolve before delivery. Recovery persists through the remainder of pregnancy. The trial meets prespecified maternal, fetal and neonatal safety criteria. Achievement applies only to the studied disease subgroup.
completion.set_by: Atlas working definition; no outside body’s published antenatal-reversal test was identified.
completion.basis: WHO defines desired treatment outcomes for pre-eclampsia, including extended pregnancy and fewer serious complications. PI4 measures time to birth and censors planned induction at 37 weeks without another indication. Neither specifies a test of sustained placental recovery. In superimposed pre-eclampsia, ISSHP distinguishes new disease manifestations from underlying chronic hypertension. The combined reversal criterion remains an Atlas working definition.

milestones.title: A treatment increases fetal growth in an animal model of placental insufficiency.
milestones.criterion: In a controlled animal model of fetal growth restriction caused by placental insufficiency, fetuses in treated pregnancies show greater growth than fetuses in control pregnancies. Serial ultrasound measurements of fetal abdominal circumference can establish a difference in growth velocity.
milestones.set_by: EVERREST consortium’s published translational programme; this proof-of-principle criterion was written for placental fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: uterine artery injection of Ad.VEGF-A165 improves fetal growth.

milestones.title: Nonclinical results support starting a pregnancy trial of a placental-disease treatment.
milestones.criterion: The sponsor provides animal or in-vitro pharmacology and toxicology data sufficient to conclude that the proposed clinical investigation is reasonably safe. The evidence addresses effects on reproduction and the developing fetus as appropriate to the drug, the phase of investigation and the proposed exposure.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8), the nonclinical evidence requirement for an investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: An early-phase study treats established placental disease and assesses maternal and fetal safety.
milestones.criterion: Pregnant participants receive the intervention after diagnosis, and the study assesses prespecified safety outcomes for the mother and fetus or infant. In SAVE phases A and B, adverse events and serious adverse events are assessed through the visit 6 weeks after delivery (±14 days). In the DM199 phase II cohorts, common primary outcomes include safety, tolerability and cord-blood drug concentration at birth.
milestones.set_by: SAVE clinical investigation plan M-2016-313, phases A and B, for preterm pre-eclampsia. The DM199 phase I/II protocol also includes a preterm fetal growth restriction cohort.
milestones.threshold_quote: in the pregnant subjects and the fetus or infant until the 6 weeks (± 14 days) post-delivery visit is reached (Phase A-B).

milestones.title: A randomized trial shows pregnancy prolongation after treatment of placental disease at α=0.05.
milestones.criterion: In a randomized superiority trial, time from randomization to birth is longer with treatment than with control in the intention-to-treat analysis at α=0.05. PI4 measures this interval in hours among women with preterm pre-eclampsia selected for expectant management. Its primary analysis censors planned induction at 37 weeks without another maternal or fetal indication and treats fetal death as interval-censored. UK STRIDER uses the randomization-to-delivery interval for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction.
milestones.set_by: PI4 steering committee, published protocol NCT06033131, for preeclampsia at 22 weeks 0 days–33 weeks 6 days; UK STRIDER independently used pregnancy duration for placental fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome is prolongation of gestation, defined as the time in hours from randomisation to birth.

milestones.title: Treatment reduces perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity in early fetal growth restriction (P<0.05).
milestones.criterion: In a randomized trial of severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, the treatment group has a lower risk of the composite of perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity through hospital discharge at two-sided P<0.05. Qualifying morbidity is grade ≥3 intraventricular haemorrhage, grade ≥2 periventricular leukomalacia, moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia, Bell stage ≥2 necrotizing enterocolitis, or retinopathy of prematurity requiring laser therapy.
milestones.set_by: Dutch STRIDER investigators, registered protocol NCT02277132 and published statistical analysis; this composite was defined for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome was a composite of either perinatal mortality or major neonatal morbidity before the neonate was discharged from the hospital.

milestones.title: In a randomized trial, fetal growth accelerates in more treated pregnancies than controls (P<0.05).
milestones.criterion: In singleton pregnancies with severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, compare the proportions with increased fetal abdominal circumference growth velocity after randomization. Express daily growth relative to that expected at the 50th centile for gestational age and compare it with pretreatment velocity. Use the day-14 scan or, after earlier delivery, the longest available interval of 10, 5 or 2 days. The treated proportion must exceed the control proportion at two-sided P<0.05.
milestones.set_by: STRIDER New Zealand and Australia investigators, protocol version 4, ACTRN12612000584831.
milestones.threshold_quote: The proportions with increased AC growth velocity in the sildenafil group and placebo group will be compared.

milestones.title: Treatment produces a clinically significant reduction in serious maternal outcomes of pre-eclampsia.
milestones.criterion: Treatment of established pre-eclampsia produces a clinically significant reduction in serious adverse maternal outcomes attributable to disease progression before or after birth. Qualifying outcomes include death, severe hypertension, significant end-organ dysfunction, eclampsia and stroke. WHO specifies clinical significance without a numerical minimum effect size.
milestones.set_by: World Health Organization, Target product profile for drugs to treat pre-eclampsia, efficacy characteristics.
milestones.threshold_quote: Clinically significant reduction in serious adverse maternal antenatal or postpartum outcomes

not_found: The EVERREST final report did not state the animal sample size for its Good Laboratory Practice reproductive toxicology study.
No statement opposing the pursuit of antenatal reversal was identified in WHO, ISUOG or SMFM guidance.
No adopted test of sustained antenatal placental recovery was identified in WHO or society guidance or in the PI4, SAVE and STRIDER protocols.

results.detail: Treatment also partly restored litter size, which can increase total litter weight independently of individual fetal growth.

results.finding: Healthy pregnant mice (sample size unstated) showed minimal evidence of dose-dependent toxicity at 6 hours.
results.detail: The fetal reporter result addresses detectable expression under the tested conditions. Developmental safety after therapeutic exposure remains unestablished.

results.finding: In rats with reduced uterine perfusion, mean fetal weight was 0.23 g higher with siRNA (7 treated vs 6 untreated dams).
results.detail: The authors describe this model as closer to late-onset preeclampsia. Dosing preceded the surgical reduction in uterine perfusion.
results.quote: Although the effect of siRNA treatment on fetal weights in the RUPP group did not reach significance in comparison with untreated RUPP, the weights were also no longer significantly different from NP.

results.finding: In the transgenic preeclampsia model, siRNA was below the 1.3 ng/g quantification limit in fetal liver (n=8).
results.detail: Developmental assessments covered selected endpoints through three weeks after birth. The authors report unexplained increases in fetal liver angiotensinogen expression in the transgenic model.
results.quote: siRNA concentrations were below the limit of quantification in fetal liver, while maternal liver contained high levels of siRNA

results.finding: In the transgenic preeclampsia model, siRNA lowered day-16 mean arterial pressure by 17.80 mmHg (9 treated vs 5 control dams).
results.detail: The study measured mean arterial pressure and renal markers. It did not report severe-hypertension events or other qualifying serious maternal outcomes.
results.quote:
Silencing of
hAGT
prevented the increase in blood pressure in the last trimester of pregnancy (MAP on day 16 of gestation: 156.24 ± 1.89 mmHg luciferase vs. 138.44 ± 1.81 mmHg
hAgt
RNAi)

results.finding: Direct placental IGF1 increased male guinea pig fetal weight versus nutrient-restricted sham controls (5 treated and 6 sham pregnancies, P=0.036).
results.detail: Only male fetuses received direct treatment. Weight increases after indirect exposure were statistically inconclusive in both sexes.
results.quote:
Fetuses whose placenta received direct nanoparticle-mediated
IGF1
injection (males only directly treated) weighed significantly more than MNR males (
P
= 0.036) and the same as control males.

results.finding: Repeated placental IGF1 nanoparticle treatment in guinea pigs (5 analyzed treated pregnancies) resulted in zero observed fetal losses.
results.detail: The study ended at near-term necropsy. The authors describe primate studies of dose, delivery and safety as underway.
results.quote:
Repeated nanoparticle-mediated
IGF1
treatments from mid pregnancy to near term resulted in no maternal health complications, no fetal loss, and no placental hemorrhage.

results.finding: In 45 randomized sheep pregnancies modeling placental fetal growth restriction, Ad.VEGF increased fetal abdominal growth versus control vector at 4 weeks (P=0.016).
results.detail: The ultrasound difference was no longer significant at the final scan, and mean fetal weight at necropsy did not differ significantly from either high-intake control group.
results.quote: The most important finding of this study is that Ad.VEGF treatment midpregnancy improves prenatal growth velocity in a well-characterized ovine paradigm of uteroplacental FGR.

results.finding: Among 57 sheep pregnancies, including 18 treated with Ad.VEGF, there were zero maternal or fetal complications during surgery or postoperative recovery.
results.detail: Follow-up ended at scheduled fetal necropsy before labor. The paper reports funding for full reproductive toxicology studies and a phase I/IIa trial.
results.quote: There were no adverse maternal or fetal complications during the surgery or the postoperative recovery period.

results.finding: DM199 reproductive toxicology found no adverse effects on fetal development in 2 animal species. Animal counts were unreported.
results.detail: The approval covers the proposed phase I/II investigation, including an expectant-management cohort with preeclampsia before 33 weeks.
results.quote: These studies showed no adverse effects on fetal development, offspring (followed for two generations) or future fertility.

results.finding: DM199 reproductive toxicology found no adverse effects on fetal development in 2 animal species. Animal counts were unreported.
results.detail: The approval covers the proposed phase I/II investigation, including an expectant-management cohort with preterm fetal growth restriction.
results.quote: These studies showed no adverse effects on fetal development, offspring (followed for two generations) or future fertility.

results.finding: VEGF gene therapy improved fetal growth in 2 preclinical FGR models. Animal sample sizes were unspecified.
results.quote: Within 2 years, the collaboration had shown proof of principle, that uterine artery injection of Ad.VEGF-A165 improves fetal growth.

results.finding: Across 8 perfused human placentas, 4 of 116 samples tested positive for the vector.
results.detail: The clinical trial application was still in final internal review. The EMA orphan designation concerned disease rarity and unmet need.
results.quote: They demonstrated minimal transfer of vector across 8 human placentas (only 4 samples out of 116 samples tested positive for vector) with minimal signs of toxicity.

results.finding: TADAFER phase II (n=87 in the safety analysis) recorded zero severe adverse events above grade 3 attributed to tadalafil.
results.detail: Transient grade 1 headache, flushing, and nasal hemorrhage were more frequent with tadalafil. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn occurred in two infants in each arm.
results.quote: No severe adverse event (>Grade 3) associated with tadalafil administration were observed in this study.

results.finding: TADAFER singleton FGR pregnancies (n=79) had higher mean two-week fetal weight growth with tadalafil (P=0.02).
results.detail: The interval began at treatment initiation. The efficacy outcomes were analyzed post hoc after enrollment stopped early.

results.finding: TADAFER (n=79 in Table 8) found a longer mean treatment-start-to-birth interval with tadalafil, with P=0.11.
results.detail: The prose describes the overall comparison as an analysis of all cases. Table 8 gives the same values under the secondary analysis headings of 40 tadalafil and 39 control pregnancies.

results.finding: TADAFER (n=87 in the safety analysis) found fewer fetal, neonatal, or infant deaths with tadalafil (P=0.03).
results.detail: The broader mortality endpoint included control deaths at 98 and 167 days. Separate morbidity counts do not establish the risk of the required composite.
results.quote:
The most important result of this safety evaluation study is the significant decrease in fetal, neonatal, and infantile deaths in the tadalafil group to the conventional treatment group: 1/44 (2%) vs. 7/43 (16%), respectively (
p
= 0.03).

results.finding: In 100 pregnancies with preeclampsia, perinatal morbidity, mortality and adverse effects did not differ between sildenafil and placebo.
results.detail: The source gives no event counts or effect estimates for the safety comparison.
results.quote: There was no difference in perinatal morbidity, mortality, or adverse effects between groups.

results.finding: In 100 pregnancies with preeclampsia, sildenafil prolonged time from randomization to delivery by about 4 days.
results.quote: Therapy with sildenafil citrate was associated with pregnancy prolongation of approximately 4 days compared with placebo in women with preeclampsia.

results.finding: In a 100-pregnancy preeclampsia trial, mean maternal blood pressure fell by 16.1 mm Hg within the sildenafil arm by 24 hours.
results.detail: The reported P values compare blood pressure over time within each arm. The source gives no comparative event rates for severe hypertension or other qualifying serious maternal outcomes.
results.quote: Maternal blood pressure before and 24 hours after randomization was lower with sildenafil (sildenafil: 100.3±5.6 mm Hg compared with 116.4±5.1 mm Hg, P<.05; placebo: 110.6±6.2 mm Hg compared with 114.7±6.5 mm Hg, P=.21).

results.finding: In 40 pregnancies with early-onset fetal growth restriction, headache was reported in 20% of women assigned nitroglycerin plus oral hydration.
results.detail: The primary endpoint was fetal growth at two weeks. Maternal vital signs and specific side effects were secondary outcomes, and neonatal outcomes were recorded at delivery.
results.quote:
Maternal side effects, summarized in Table
5
, indicated that side effects such as headache, palpitation, and postural hypotension were slightly more common in Group A compared to Group B, but none of these differences were statistically significance, with all P values are greater than 0.05.

results.finding: In 40 randomized pregnancies with early-onset fetal growth restriction, mean fetal abdominal circumference at two weeks favored treatment (P=0.041).
results.detail: The reported eligibility criteria covered several early-onset fetal growth restriction presentations. The authors state that enrolled participants had forward umbilical artery end-diastolic flow.
results.quote:
After a two-week period, Group A showed significant improvements in EFW, AC, HC, BPD, FL, amniotic fluid index, and UA Doppler PI with P values 0.032, 0.041, 0.010, 0.011, 0.038, 0.037, 0.042, respectively as shown in Table
2
.

results.finding: In 40 randomized pregnancies with early-onset fetal growth restriction, the mean delivery interval favored nitroglycerin plus oral hydration (P=0.048).
results.detail: Table 3 gives group means and a t-test P value without specifying the denominator for the delivery-interval analysis.
results.quote: the mean latency to delivery was significantly longer compared to Group B.

results.finding: In 40 randomized pregnancies with early-onset fetal growth restriction, the neonatal death comparison yielded P=0.375.
results.quote: Conversely, there were no statistically significant difference regarding the mode of delivery, incidence of IUFD, fetal distress, and neonatal death with P values 0.16, 0.151, 0.102, and 0.375, respectively.

results.finding: Selective apheresis reduced circulating sFlt-1 by about 50% in pregnant baboons. Sample size was unspecified.
results.detail: The excerpt lists a supplementary baboon study report but provides no reproductive or fetal safety results from it.
results.quote: Extracorporeal apheresis with an adsorber containing high-affinity IgG1 antibodies against sFlt-1 resulted in an approximately 50% reduction of circulating sFlt-1 levels in pregnant baboons.

results.finding: In the SAVE pilot of apheresis for preterm preeclampsia (n=16), mild hypocalcemia was reported in 3 participants.
results.detail: The excerpt lists a long-term maternal and infant follow-up table without specifying the timing or scope of adverse-event ascertainment.
results.quote:
Treatment-related adverse events included mild hypocalcemia (
n
= 3), skin hemorrhage at the puncture site (
n
= 1) and false labor (
n
= 1).

results.finding: In very preterm preeclampsia, the delivery hazard ratio was 0.14 for phase B apheresis recipients (n=9) versus untreated women (n=16).
results.quote: Kaplan-Meier survival curve showing time to delivery is depicted for treated (N = 9 in Phase B) and untreated women (N = 16) (Hazard ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.04–0.50, P = 0.0003).

results.finding: In very preterm preeclampsia (phase B, n=9), mean arterial pressure fell by 4.1 mmHg per apheresis on average.
results.detail: The reported outcome was the immediate change in mean arterial pressure. Rates of severe hypertension before or after delivery were unreported.
results.quote: each apheresis reduced sFlt-1 levels by 16.7 ± 7.6% and mean arterial pressures by 4.1 ± 7.8 mmHg.

results.finding: Etanercept increased gestational day-20 viable fetal weight in rats with reduced uterine perfusion (8 dams per arm, P = 0.0480).
results.detail: Fetal weight was averaged per dam among viable fetuses. The analysis included litters with viable offspring.
results.quote: Average fetal weight per dam was significantly increased in viable offspring from Etan-RUPP compared to RUPP (p=0.0480)

results.finding: Fetal survival remained lower in etanercept-treated rats with reduced uterine perfusion (8 dams) than in vehicle-treated sham rats (9 dams, P < 0.0001).
results.detail: The survival P value compares treated diseased dams with sham controls. The study reported no improvement in fetal survival with etanercept in diseased dams.
results.quote: Fetal survival ratio at G20 was significantly reduced in RUPP (p = 0.0002) and Etan-RUPP (p < 0.0001) compared to Sham.

results.finding: Among 66 antithrombin recipients with severe preeclampsia, zero treatment-related adverse events were reported.
results.detail: The trial also measured fetal biophysical profiles and estimated fetal weight gain. The abstract describes these as fetal assessments without identifying them as prespecified safety outcomes.
results.quote: No adverse events related to AT were observed.

results.finding: Antithrombin prolonged gestation versus placebo in a randomized trial of 133 patients with severe preeclampsia (P=0.007).
results.detail: The abstract does not quantify the prolongation or specify whether it measured the interval from randomization to birth.
results.quote: Gestation was significantly prolonged (p = 0.007), and the number of low-birth weight infants was significantly smaller (p = 0.011) in the AT group.

results.finding: In 133 patients with severe preeclampsia, antithrombin improved the maternal Gestosis Index more than placebo (P=0.020).
results.detail: The abstract reports a change in the overall score and gives no comparative rates of severe hypertension, significant end-organ dysfunction, eclampsia, stroke, or maternal death.
results.quote: Improvement was significantly greater in the AT group for both the GI (p = 0.020) and the estimated fetal weight gain (p = 0.029).

results.finding: In severe early preeclampsia (n=181), maternal hemorrhage-related adverse events were 19.0 percentage points more frequent with rhAT-gamma than with placebo.
results.detail: The 95% CI for the hemorrhage-related adverse event difference was 4.3 to 32.7 percentage points.
results.quote: AEs were observed in 70/91 (76.9%) patients, 28/91 (30.8%) fetuses, and 30/91 (33.0%) neonates in the placebo group and in 69/90 (76.7%) patients, 26/90 (28.9%) fetuses, and 34/90 (37.8%) neonates in the rhAT-gamma group.

results.finding: In severe early preeclampsia (n=181 analyzed), rhAT-gamma versus placebo yielded P=0.07 for time from treatment initiation to delivery.
results.detail: The two untreated participants were excluded after worsening maternal and fetal condition.
results.quote:
There was no statistically significant difference in the pregnancy period between the placebo and rhAT-gamma groups (
P
=0.07).

results.finding: In early preeclampsia, the primary comparison of metformin versus placebo favored longer gestation (180 randomized, 179 analyzed, P=0.057).
results.detail: Expectant management ended at 34 weeks. The source does not report PI4's censoring rules for planned 37-week induction or fetal death. The statistically significant adherence analyses address per-protocol effects.
results.quote: a median difference of 7.6 days (geometric mean ratio 1.39, 95% confidence interval 0.99 to 1.95; P=0.057).

results.finding: In severe early-onset fetal growth restriction (n=135), sildenafil showed no significant prolongation of time from randomization to delivery (p=0.23).
results.detail: The linear regression comparison also fell short of statistical significance (p=0.19).
results.quote:
We found no difference in the median randomisation to delivery interval between women 
assigned to sildenafil (17 days [IQR 7–24]) and women assigned to placebo (18 days [8–28]; p=0·23).

results.finding: In severe early-onset placental fetal growth restriction (216 randomized), the relative risk of perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity with sildenafil versus placebo was 1.11.
results.detail: The trial stopped early because of a neonatal pulmonary hypertension safety signal and low likelihood of benefit on the primary outcome. One placebo participant was lost to follow-up.
results.quote: The primary outcome, perinatal mortality or major neonatal morbidity, occurred in the offspring of 65 participants (60.2%) allocated to sildenafil vs 58 participants (54.2%) allocated to placebo (relative risk, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.88-1.40;  P  = .38).

results.finding: In severe early-onset fetal growth restriction (118 evaluable pregnancies), growth velocity increased in 15.9 percentage points fewer pregnancies with sildenafil than with placebo.
results.detail: Four of the 122 randomized pregnancies lacked a post-treatment growth measurement because delivery or fetal death occurred within 48 hours.
results.quote:
Sildenafil did not affect the proportion of pregnancies with an increase in fetal growth 
velocity; 32/61 (52.5%) sildenafil-treated and 39/57 (68.4%) placebo-treated, adjusted OR 0.49, 95% 
CI 0.23-1.05.

results.finding: In 2,412 women with pre-eclampsia enrolled before 34 weeks, the relative risk of eclampsia with magnesium sulphate versus placebo was 0.54.
results.detail: Figure 2 reports the subgroup estimate. The trial-wide reduction was statistically significant, but that estimate pooled women across gestational ages and included postpartum enrollment.

results.finding: In 160 women with early preeclampsia, esomeprazole reduced maternal fits by 17.5 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The Results report 27.5% for control-group fits, while the Discussion gives 22%. The finding uses the Results figure.
results.quote:
Concerning the reported maternal adverse 
events, women in the intervention group had a significantly lower 
incidence of fits compared to those in the control group (10% vs. 
27.5%, P=0.005) (Figure 2).

goal.need = "A 2019 estimate put severe early-onset fetal growth restriction at 11,000 babies a year in the EU. A fetus receiving too little oxygen risks brain injury or stillbirth. Delivering very early adds risks of brain haemorrhage and chronic lung disease. In pre-eclampsia, blood-pressure treatment and seizure prevention protect the mother while the placenta can continue to drive disease. Restoring placental support could give the baby time to grow and mature, provided both mother and fetus can safely continue the pregnancy.". Reason: The current rationale points to absent global figures and omits the trade-off families face when delivery is the only way to stop deterioration.

add statement by World Health Organization, 2023: "delay or stop maternal disease progression". Reason: WHO explicitly names halting established maternal disease as a drug-development goal for pre-eclampsia.

edit completion: criterion = "In pregnancies with established placental insufficiency, a randomized controlled trial demonstrates recovery of placental support sufficient to sustain fetal growth and remove the disease indication for delivery before 37 weeks. Where pre-eclampsia is present, the hypertension, proteinuria and other organ dysfunction attributable to pre-eclampsia resolve before delivery. Recovery persists through the remainder of pregnancy. The trial meets prespecified maternal, fetal and neonatal safety criteria. Achievement applies only to the studied disease subgroup."; basis = "WHO defines desired treatment outcomes for pre-eclampsia, including extended pregnancy and fewer serious complications. PI4 measures time to birth and censors planned induction at 37 weeks without another indication. Neither specifies a test of sustained placental recovery. In superimposed pre-eclampsia, ISSHP distinguishes new disease manifestations from underlying chronic hypertension. The combined reversal criterion remains an Atlas working definition."; refs = [2, 4, 6, 7, 25, 26]. Reason: Requiring all maternal hypertension to resolve would incorrectly require treatment to cure pre-existing chronic hypertension in women with superimposed pre-eclampsia.

edit m1: criterion = "In a controlled animal model of fetal growth restriction caused by placental insufficiency, fetuses in treated pregnancies show greater growth than fetuses in control pregnancies. Serial ultrasound measurements of fetal abdominal circumference can establish a difference in growth velocity.". Reason: The sheep experiment's sample sizes and findings obscure the reusable test for improved fetal growth.

edit m2: criterion = "The sponsor provides animal or in-vitro pharmacology and toxicology data sufficient to conclude that the proposed clinical investigation is reasonably safe. The evidence addresses effects on reproduction and the developing fetus as appropriate to the drug, the phase of investigation and the proposed exposure.". Reason: The FDA requirement concerns the evidence supporting the sponsor's safety judgment, while the current criterion also reports one programme's findings.

edit m3: title = "An early-phase study treats established placental disease and assesses maternal and fetal safety."; criterion = "Pregnant participants receive the intervention after diagnosis, and the study assesses prespecified safety outcomes for the mother and fetus or infant. In SAVE phases A and B, adverse events and serious adverse events are assessed through the visit 6 weeks after delivery (\u00b114 days). In the DM199 phase II cohorts, common primary outcomes include safety, tolerability and cord-blood drug concentration at birth."; set_by = "SAVE clinical investigation plan M-2016-313, phases A and B, for preterm pre-eclampsia. The DM199 phase I/II protocol also includes a preterm fetal growth restriction cohort."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "in the pregnant subjects and the fetus or infant until the 6 weeks (\u00b1 14 days) post-delivery visit is reached (Phase A-B)."; threshold_ref = 28; refs = [28, 10, 18]. Reason: The SAVE and DM199 protocols specify what safety follow-up entails in the two presentations, which participant counts alone cannot establish.

add milestone after m3: "In a randomized trial, fetal growth accelerates in more treated pregnancies than controls (P<0.05).". Reason: The entry tracks fetal growth in animals but omits the randomized human test of whether growth accelerates before birth.

edit m4: criterion = "In a randomized superiority trial, time from randomization to birth is longer with treatment than with control in the intention-to-treat analysis at \u03b1=0.05. PI4 measures this interval in hours among women with preterm pre-eclampsia selected for expectant management. Its primary analysis censors planned induction at 37 weeks without another maternal or fetal indication and treats fetal death as interval-censored. UK STRIDER uses the randomization-to-delivery interval for severe early-onset fetal growth restriction."; refs = [7, 13]. Reason: The primary endpoint needs its time origin and analysis population, while the PI2 and UK STRIDER results belong with the evidence.

edit m5: title = "Treatment reduces perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity in early fetal growth restriction (P<0.05)."; criterion = "In a randomized trial of severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, the treatment group has a lower risk of the composite of perinatal death or major neonatal morbidity through hospital discharge at two-sided P<0.05. Qualifying morbidity is grade \u22653 intraventricular haemorrhage, grade \u22652 periventricular leukomalacia, moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia, Bell stage \u22652 necrotizing enterocolitis, or retinopathy of prematurity requiring laser therapy."; threshold_quote = "The primary outcome was a composite of either perinatal mortality or major neonatal morbidity before the neonate was discharged from the hospital."; threshold_ref = 14; refs = [14]. Reason: The Dutch STRIDER composite has a defined follow-up period and morbidity grades that can be stated independently of the trial results.

add milestone after m5: "Treatment produces a clinically significant reduction in serious maternal outcomes of pre-eclampsia.". Reason: The clinical milestones omit WHO's maternal efficacy outcome for pre-eclampsia, which pregnancy duration and infant outcomes cannot measure.
remove not found 0. Reason: Report 3 in the published supplement contains both the SAVE clinical investigation plan and its statistical analysis plan.

add not found: "No statement opposing the pursuit of antenatal reversal was identified in WHO, ISUOG or SMFM guidance.". Reason: The available institutional statements address current therapies and development goals without establishing opposition to the goal itself.

add not found: "No adopted test of sustained antenatal placental recovery was identified in WHO or society guidance or in the PI4, SAVE and STRIDER protocols.". Reason: The WHO product profile and registered trial protocols define intermediate outcomes but leave the combined reversal test without an external authority.
